personal_reading_notes: I understand the motivating contrast: a person might understand 臺北 and 台北 as the same place, but exact copying treats 臺 and 台 as different characters.
OCR is described as recognizing text in an image. The prose separates exact character transcription, text presence, and unreadable visible text.
CER counts the least number of changes needed to convert the prediction to the reference, divided by the reference length. It can count missing or additional characters as well as substitutions.
The five reference characters are 今, 天, 去, 臺, 北. 台 replacing 臺 requires one substitution, so CER is 1/5=0.2.

The import brings in text_error_report; the call compares two strings; report holds named fields and the print lines display exact-match status, edit count, reference length, and CER. 11.16 explains dictionary lookup by the quoted field names.
Unicode characters are the unit used here; byte counts used to store the string are a different measurement and do not change the five-character denominator.
Normalization means deciding beforehand how strings should be standardized. The NFKC fullwidth A example is concrete, and the prose explicitly says it does not map 臺 to 台.
For an empty reference CER has no denominator, so presence/absence needs a separate test. Blurred unreadable text should not be classified as a blank image.
Synthetic documents control fonts and answers; real signs bring perspective, glare and background variation. Separate results and page/short-line scope make this comparison interpretable.
